implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library puts the operations directly on Iterable: map, filter, flatMap, distinct, sortedBy, groupBy, take, and fold/reduce/sum/sumOf as terminals. The docs describe this processing as eager - 'each processing step completes and returns its result - an intermediate collection' - which replaces the classic loop with a chain of library calls while keeping every intermediate inspectable. The eager form is the default and usually wins for small collections, where the documentation explicitly warns that laziness adds overhead.
code_sketch:
val emails = people
    .filter { it.isActive }
    .map { it.email }
    .distinct()
    .sorted()
    .take(10)                     // eager: one list per stage

val total = orders.sumOf { it.amount }     // terminal
pitfalls: Each stage allocates a new list, so a long chain over a large collection produces one intermediate collection per stage.
map/filter on a MutableList-typed receiver still return new lists: mutating the elements inside the lambdas mutates the shared objects (aliasing), not copies.

variants.name: Lazy sequences (asSequence)
variants.idiom_name: Sequence operators via asSequence() / sequence { yield(...) }
variants.implementation_notes: asSequence() switches the same operator names to lazy per-element evaluation: the docs state that 'multistep processing of sequences is executed lazily when possible: actual computing happens only when the result of the whole processing chain is requested', that all steps run one by one for each element, and that no intermediate results are built - so a take(4) stops pulling after the fourth survivor. The same page notes the lazy nature adds overhead that can dominate on small collections. Use it for large sources, long chains and short-circuiting tails.
pitfalls: Without a terminal operation (toList, first, sum, forEach) nothing runs at all.
A Sequence is single-use: iterating the same sequence twice re-evaluates the whole chain, and a sequence {} builder re-runs its side effects each time.

variants.name: Asynchronous flows (kotlinx.coroutines)
variants.implementation_notes: When the elements arrive asynchronously, the same operators exist on Flow: the docs describe a flow as 'a sequential stream of values that can be produced asynchronously', with intermediate operators (map, filter, transform) returning another cold flow and terminal operators (collect, toList, fold, reduce) starting the work, and note that 'like sequences, cold flows are lazy'. On top of the sequence model it adds suspension, structured cancellation and buffering operators (buffer, flowOn, flatMapMerge) that plain sequences cannot express. Choose it for I/O-bound element pipelines; keep the suspend-free forms for in-memory data.
pitfalls: Hot flows (SharedFlow/StateFlow) are shared and not lazy per collector, so replacing a cold flow with a hot one changes when and how often the upstream runs.
Flow operators are sequential by default; concurrency requires explicit operators (buffer/flatMapMerge) and shared mutable state must still be avoided.
Exceptions in a flow travel through the collector and cancel the scope: without a catch/retry operator a single failed element aborts the whole pipeline.
